messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya Subramaniam is a 66-year-old South Asian woman who works as a security guard at a mid-sized shopping complex in the suburbs of Houston. She has been married for over forty years, and until approximately eighteen months ago, she would have described her life as quietly full. That changed on a Tuesday afternoon when her son, Kiran, was struck by a driver who ran a red light at an intersection Priya knew well — one she had suggested he use as a shortcut when he called her from the road that day. He was airlifted to the hospital and survived, but sustained a traumatic brain injury that left him with lasting cognitive impairment. Priya was the last person who spoke to him before the crash. She had told him to take that route.

In the weeks that followed the accident, Priya sat at Kiran's bedside through the acute phase of his hospitalization, and it was there that something shifted in her that she could not name at the time. She began replaying the phone call obsessively — her own voice, the specific words she used, the confident way she had directed him. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unshakeable, that she was the reason this had happened. Not the driver, not the light, not chance — her. She had failed to protect her child, and the evidence, as she experienced it, was irrefutable.

When Kiran was eventually discharged to a rehabilitation facility, Priya returned to work. The shopping complex where she patrols has a large car park, and several times each shift she watches vehicles maneuver through tight spaces, hears the occasional screech of brakes, or passes colleagues talking about fender-benders on the morning commute. Each of these moments arrives in her body before it arrives in her mind — a sudden surge of heat, her heart slamming against her chest, her hands going rigid on the radio at her hip. The memory of Kiran's voice cutting out mid-sentence does not feel like something that happened eighteen months ago; it feels like it is happening at the exact moment she hears tires on asphalt, immediate and total, pulling her out of the present entirely. When it comes on fully she has to step into a stairwell and press her back against the wall until it passes, because the emotion that accompanies it is so overwhelming she cannot continue to function. She has told no one at work why she disappears.

Outside of work, Priya has quietly reorganized her life around what she cannot bear. She stopped attending the temple events she once looked forward to, because a close family friend lost her husband last spring and Priya cannot be near grief — flowers arranged for mourning, the particular stillness of a room where someone is being remembered — without her body responding as though she herself is standing at the edge of something catastrophic. She declined the invitation to the friend's husband's memorial without explanation. Her husband has noticed that she deflects any conversation that carries even the faint possibility of disagreement, retreating from the room or changing the subject before tension can gather. He has begun to move around her carefully, and the distance between them has grown in ways neither of them has yet spoken aloud.

Priya keeps her body in a state of continuous readiness. At the security desk, in the car park, in the supermarket — her eyes move constantly, cataloguing exits, watching for anything that might signal something about to go wrong. She tries, with considerable effort, not to think about the accident directly, pushing the images away when they surface. What frightens her most is not the intrusions themselves but what she has concluded from them: that she is no longer capable of feeling ordinary warmth or ease, that something in her that used to be available to her family has been permanently closed off.

She came to seek help after Kiran asked her, during one of her visits, why she seemed so far away. She could not answer him. What she hopes for, though she can barely articulate it, is some way back to being present in her own life. What she fears is that she has already proven she does not deserve it.
